title: Infra Engineering: GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts, IaC, CI/CD & Runbooks
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview

This document describes Redwood Inference engineering standards and runbook guidance for: GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC modules and workflows, CI/CD for infra and inference images, and operational runbooks maintained in the infra team wiki. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners.

Scope
- GPU fleet architecture and provisioning (Hosted + Dedicated pools)
- Cloud account topology and network primitives (VPCs, Transit GW, peering)
- Terraform module standards, versioning, and registry practices
- CI/CD pipelines for infra (Terraform), runtime images, and integration tests
- Runbooks for common incidents (capacity exhaustion, node failures, OOMs)
- Team wiki hygiene and ownership model

1) GPU Fleet & Capacity

Summary
- Fleet spans dedicated GPU pools for Dedicated customers and shared pools for hosted traffic. Primary instance families: NVIDIA A10G, A100, H100 (where available). Use mixed instance pools to improve scheduling flexibility.

Fleet topology and naming
- Accounts: gpu-hosted-prod, gpu-dedicated-prod, gpu-staging. Each account contains 1+ auto-scaling ASGs/managed node groups per region and per instance-family.
- Node labels: node.k8s.redwood/gpu-family, node.k8s.redwood/pool-tier (hosted|dedicated), node.k8s.redwood/gpu-count

Capacity planning metrics (tracked per region and pool)
- Desired utilization: 55-70% (steady-state)
- Burst headroom target: 20% reserved for sudden demand spikes
- Cold-start threshold: scale-up when avg GPU queue depth > 12 for 2 consecutive minutes
- SLOs: 99.5% request success (no capacity queueing) and 95th percentile latency under target for each plan tier

Capacity dashboard & alerts
- Grafana dashboards: infra/gpu/capacity-overview, infra/gpu/queue-latency, infra/gpu/evictions
- PagerDuty: PD escalation policy "GPU Capacity" (SEV1 for >10% of requests queued >2m)
- Alert examples:
  - gpu_queue_depth_high: triggers when queue_depth_percentile(95m) > 80% for 3m
  - node_gpu_memory_pressure: node GPU memory > 92% for 3m -> auto-eviction remediation runbook

Operational commands
- List nodes by GPU family (kubectl):
  kubectl get nodes -l node.k8s.redwood/gpu-family=A100 -o wide
- Query pending pods with GPU requests:
  kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].resources.requests.nvidia.com/gpu!=null)'

Autoscaling policy (recommended)
1. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for model servers (requests per GPU core metric)
2. Cluster AutoScaler tuned with GPU bin-packing (scale up when unschedulable pods > 1 for 2m)
3. Predictive scale-plan job runs every 4h using historical traces to pre-warm capacity for scheduled traffic spikes

Cost controls and quotas
- Use per-pool tags and CostCenter labels to attribute spend. Default nightly scale-down window: 00:00-05:00 local to region (configurable per-customer).
- Reserved capacity for Dedicated contracts managed via dedicated ASGs with min-size equal to contracted baseline.

2) Cloud Accounts & Networking

Account topology (recommended pattern)
- Organization root -> shared-services -> prod -> staging -> dev -> dedicated-customers
- Shared-services hosts IAM, logging (central ELK), security tooling, and CI runners
- Each prod account has dedicated VPCs per region and Transit Gateway for cross-region connectivity where needed

Network primitives and conventions
- VPC CIDR allocations: use /16 per account with /24 subnets per AZ for workload and /28 for bastion/control-plane networks. Maintain an allocation table in the wiki.
- Subnet naming: {env}-{region}-{az}-{purpose} (e.g., prod-us-west-2a-workload)
- Egress patterns: NAT Gateway for private subnets; prefer Egress-only endpoints for IPv6 where available
- PrivateLink for service endpoints (e.g., S3, ECR) to avoid transit over public internet

Security & IAM baseline
- No root usage in day-to-day ops. Use IAM roles with short-lived STS credentials via SSO.
- Baseline role names: infra-admin, infra-readonly, deployer, monitoring-agent
- KMS key policy patterns: separate keys per-account for audit separation; central key rotation cadence documented in security docs

VPC peering and Transit Gateway guidance
- Use Transit Gateway for many-to-many connectivity; prefer VPC Peering for simple two-account links. Document cost tradeoffs in the team wiki.

3) Terraform / IaC Modules

Module registry and layout
- Internal registry hosted at gitlab.com/redwood-infra/modules (monorepo per domain). Module naming: redwood-mod-{domain}-{resource} (e.g., redwood-mod-network-vpc, redwood-mod-eks-cluster).
- Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Use tags and changelogs for each module.

Module standards
- All modules must include: inputs.md, outputs.md, examples/, README with usage, and 1+ integration test in modules-ci/
- Sensitive defaults: do not set KMS keys, do not enable public access by default.
- Accept a "tags" and "cost_center" variable on all modules for unified billing tags.

Terraform workflow (CI)
1. Branch change -> pipeline runs terratest/unit checks -> terraform fmt & validate -> plan against ephemeral workspaces using tfswitch to pin versions
2. Reviewers must approve plan in merge request; pipeline enforces minimal review count and a positive plan approval
3. Merge triggers promote pipeline: apply to staging, run integration tests, promote to prod-once-manual-gate

Example module usage snippet
```hcl
module "redwood_vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@gitlab.com/redwood-infra/modules.git//network/vpc?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "prod-us-west-2"
  cidr   = "10.40.0.0/16"
  tags   = { environment = "prod", cost_center = "infra" }
}
```

Version pinning and drift management
- Use terraform lock files and provider version pins. Monthly drift scan job runs `terraform plan` across prod workspaces and creates issues for unapproved drift.

4) CI/CD and Build

Pipeline responsibilities
- Build infra plans (Terraform), run terratest, apply via runners in shared-services account
- Build and publish inference runtime images to ECR with tags: sha-<short>, release-<semver>, latest-stable when gated
- Integration tests run in ephemeral clusters populated with test model artifacts

Pipeline layout (recommended)
- repo: infra/terraform -> pipeline: lint -> unit tests -> terraform plan in ephemeral -> human approve -> apply to target account
- repo: runtime/images -> build -> security scan (Trivy) -> push to staging ECR -> deploy to staging cluster -> smoke tests -> promote

Secrets handling
- Use SSM Parameter Store / Secrets Manager in shared-services account with cross-account role access. CI runners assume role via OIDC. No long-lived static keys in repos.

Failure modes and mitigations
- If pipeline apply fails due to quota: detect error code, open incident, revert previous merge if necessary, and notify oncall.

5) Infra Runbooks (Operational Procedures)

Runbook: GPU capacity exhaustion (high-level)
1. Detect: Alert gpu_queue_depth_high fires. Confirm via Grafana (infra/gpu/queue-latency).
2. Triage: Identify affected pools (hosted vs dedicated) and regions.
3. Immediate mitigation (order matters):
   a. Scale up GPU node group for affected pool (increase ASG/min by +20%).
   b. For hosted pools, enable burst capacity lambda to provision additional instance-family nodes.
   c. If Dedicated contract affected, notify account owner and follow contract escalations.
4. Post-incident: Run capacity retro, update predictive scale rules and update runbook with root cause.

CLI examples
- Scale node group (AWS CLI + eksctl example):
  aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name redwood-gpu-a100-asg --min-size 12 --max-size 48
  eksctl scale nodegroup --cluster prod-us-west-2 --name gpu-a100 --nodes 24

Runbook: GPU OOM evictions
1. Detect: node_gpu_memory_pressure alert or pod OOMKilled events.
2. Triage: Identify pods with highest GPU memory (kubectl top pods --containers). Check model batch sizes and tensor sizes.
3. Mitigation:
   - Temporarily reduce model server batch size via runtime config (example below)
   - Evict offending pods to be rescheduled on larger-GPU nodes
   - If frequent, create an issue to add per-model quantization/half-precision profile in optimize catalog

Runtime config patch (example curl to feature-flag service):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
    -d '{"model_id":"search-v2","runtime":{"max_batch":8}}' \
    https://console.redwood.internal/api/v1/runtime-configs/patch

Runbook: Terraform apply failure due to quota
1. Detect: CI pipeline step fails with quota error.
2. Action: Identify quota namespace (EC2 GPUs, ENIs, VPCs). Request quota increase via cloud console and attach ticket to pipeline MR. If emergency, rollback merge and re-run after quota update.

6) Infra Team Wiki & Ownership

Wiki hygiene
- Owners must maintain a short summary, oncall roster, runbooks, and links to dashboards. Each page must include an owner, last-reviewed date, and escalation contacts.
- Tag pages with labels: owner-team, oncall, runbook, critical-infrastructure

Oncall & escalation
- Oncall rotation: infra-oncall-1 -> infra-oncall-2 -> infra-arch (weekly rotation). Primary oncall handles SEV1 and makes decisions for capacity changes.
- PagerDuty escalation policy mapping and Slack channel #infra-ops must be listed on each runbook page.

Ownership table (example)
| Area | Primary Owner | Secondary Owner | PagerDuty Policy | Runbook Link |
|------|---------------|-----------------|------------------|--------------|
| GPU Fleet | Maya Patel | Diego Martinez | GPU Capacity | /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-fleet-capacity-playbook |
| Terraform Modules | Avery Chen | Priya Singh | Infra CI | /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/terraform-module-registry |

Maintenance cadence
- Runbooks: review quarterly.
- Terraform modules: major releases twice per quarter; security patches as needed.
- Capacity plan: review monthly and before major sales/marketing events.
